meta.subtitle: Oct 6 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas data centers, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Abbott sold Texas to donors
lanes.description: Abbott and Texas Republicans took data center campaign money and gave away tax breaks (about $1B+ a year), so Texans pay with higher taxes, bills and a pushed-aside rural population; the freeze is election-year cover.

lanes.label: Paxton vs Talarico data center money
lanes.description: Senate race attack lines over who is the data center sellout: Democrats say Paxton traded land, water and tax breaks for contributions, while Republicans counter that Talarico and Hinojosa are funded by or voted for data centers.

lanes.label: Grid queue, speculation and pause
lanes.description: The freeze is a rational response to an ERCOT large-load queue that ballooned from 63 GW to 474 GW, mostly duplicate or speculative requests, which threatens grid reliability and electricity prices.

lanes.label: Rural land, water and nuisance
lanes.description: Data centers drain West Texas water, hurt farmers, ranchers, wildlife and dark skies, and push transmission lines onto private land, so rural communities bear the costs.

lanes.label: Secrecy and weak oversight
lanes.description: Abbott's audit and the PUC are shielding data center locations and resource use from the public (citing terrorism risk) and impose token penalties, so promised accountability is hollow.

lanes.label: AI power boom is an opportunity
lanes.description: Texas data center demand is a growth and investment story, with new power plants, behind-the-meter gas, nuclear and jobs, and even a claim that data centers can lower power bills, so the pause is a bottleneck that favors already-powered projects.

$SLNH | Kati 2: A New $472M Construction Filing in Texas

An interesting development for Soluna's Project Kati 2.

According to Rio Grande Valley Business Journal, a new filing was registered with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation on October 7, outlining a privately funded AI data center in Willacy County.

The reported figures are substantial:

- $471.8 million in estimated construction costs
- 471,884 sq. ft. of planned data center space
- 112 MW of critical IT capacity
- October 8, 2026 scheduled construction start
- October 8, 2027 scheduled completion

What stands out to me is how much more defined the physical development has become.

Soluna and Metrobloks have spent much of 2026 advancing the campus design, negotiating with prospective tenants and developing the power infrastructure. We now have a reported state registration identifying the building footprint, estimated construction cost and a specific construction schedule.

The 112 MW critical IT figure is particularly interesting, providing another reference point for the scale of the first AI development phase.

This also follows Soluna's completion of the 83 MW Kati 1 facility and ERCOT's conditional Base Load classification for the full 166 MW Kati campus.

The registration itself is not a construction permit or confirmation of financing, and the scheduled start date does not establish that physical construction has begun.

Still, I see this as another encouraging development. The project continues to take shape through increasingly concrete engineering and administrative milestones while the commercial process advances.

For us shareholders watching Kati 2 closely, this is meaningful progress ahead of the next major announcements.

Source: Rio Grande Valley Business Journal, October 7, 2026.

Paper Gigawatts

Book a restaurant for Saturday and you have a reservation.

If the place is popular, you book a second one down the street. 

Neither booking costs you a cent, and both kitchens are buying fish for you on Friday.

A demand forecast is a stack of reservations added up by someone who never checks who showed up.

The power models take reservations from the same kind of customer, and this booking is free too.

A data center developer files an interconnection request with a utility. 

Because the request costs nothing.

Te developer files several, in several states, and waits to see which grid answers first.

Texas publishes the most honest count. 

▪️ At the end of 2024, its grid operator had 63 gigawatts of large-load requests in the queue.

$SLNH | Dorothy 3 Takes Shape: A 300 MW AI Campus Built Around Flexibility and Available Power

Soluna recently published photos on LinkedIn from its Open House in Silverton, Texas, where the company introduced Project Dorothy 3 to the local community.

One of the presentation boards caught my attention. It shows a more detailed development plan for Dorothy 3 than what I've seen in the company's earlier public materials.

The proposed 300 MW AI campus is divided into three phases:

- Phase 1: 75 MW
- Phase 2: 75 MW
- Phase 3: 150 MW

The board also appears to contain information about expected completion, although the relevant details are obscured in the photograph.

The significance here isn't simply the 300 MW figure, which Soluna has discussed for some time. It's how the company appears to be planning its development.

An interesting shift in AI infrastructure demand

Two reports from September make this particularly relevant.

On September 18, CNBC reported that OpenAI and Anthropic were exploring smaller data center deployments of approximately 20–30 MW, alongside their existing commitments to much larger AI campuses.

A day earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Crusoe, the developer behind OpenAI's massive Abilene data center, was expanding into smaller, factory-built modular facilities that can be transported to locations with available electricity.

Crusoe's strategy reflects growing demand for faster capacity delivery, particularly as AI inference expands. Large training campuses remain essential, but not every computing workload requires a facility with hundreds of megawatts available from day one.

That distinction matters for Dorothy 3.

An initial 75 MW phase could allow Soluna to match construction and capital requirements more closely to contracted demand, bring capacity online in stages and expand as additional power becomes available.

This isn't confirmation that Dorothy 3 will use Crusoe-style prefabricated modules. However, its proposed phase structure is consistent with the industry's increasing emphasis on flexible capacity deployment.

Dorothy 3 already has an important foundation

Unlike developers starting with undeveloped land and no nearby generating assets, Soluna has spent much of 2026 consolidating its position around Dorothy.

The company now owns the adjacent 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm, has consolidated ownership of Dorothy 1 and completed the purchase of 397 acres for Dorothy 3.

The Briscoe substation sits directly across from the newly acquired property, providing an important starting point for the planned behind-the-meter development.

Soluna also has approximately 98 MW of existing operating infrastructure at Dorothy 1 and 2.

In September, ERCOT conditionally classified 100 MW at the existing Dorothy campus as Base Load under Batch Zero, while a separate 50 MW interconnection request remained under study. This does not constitute approval for Dorothy 3's new phases, but it highlights the value of developing alongside an established, energized campus.

There is also an important distinction between Soluna's approach and a conventional wind-only data center.

The company's strategy involves combining renewable generation with grid access and additional power resources. Soluna has discussed evaluating onsite gas generation and clustering nearby energy assets to support larger AI campuses.

That combination could be especially valuable for a phased project where power requirements increase as new data halls are developed.

The Open House photographs reveal more than the capacity plan

Another presentation board addresses the project's expected noise and nearby residences.

The material appears to reference approximately 55 dB at the facility fence, along with a map identifying one residence about 1.5 miles northeast and three residences at least 1.8 miles west of the site.

59 American data centers now plan to build their own power plants.

About 90 gigawatts' worth, led by Texas. Roughly 2 of those gigawatts are running today.

The numbers come from Cleanview, which tracks the projects. Together they make up more than a quarter of all planned data center capacity in the country. More than nine in ten were announced since the start of 2025. The Texas lead is built on Permian Basin gas.

The reason is the wait. Cleanview puts the time to connect a data center to the grid at as long as seven years. An AI company cannot wait seven years, so it builds a power plant of its own and connects to the grid later, or never.

Most of it runs on gas. In an earlier count, about three-quarters of the generating equipment Cleanview could identify was natural gas.

But announced is a press release. Energized is a construction project.

In April, Oracle's Project Jupiter campus in New Mexico swapped its planned gas turbines and diesel generators for up to 2.45 gigawatts of fuel cells. Cleanview now says the project is likely to miss its target of coming online in 2027.

Somewhere between 90 gigawatts announced and 2 running sit the contracts, the turbines on back order, the permits and the pipelines. When a project stalls between announced and energized, the first question is who was responsible for which of those.

A technology company that builds its own power plant has become a power company, with a power company's construction risk.

posts.text:
Texas oilfield wastewater could help cool data centers without draining freshwater | Muskanbhatia, Interesting Engineering

Can waste water from the oil and energy industry quench the thirst of data centers? Researchers at The University of Texas in Austin are betting it can.

They suggest that established desalination technologies could allow data centers to use salty or contaminated water to meet their cooling needs, reducing their reliance on freshwater.

Although there are various ways to separate salt from water, researchers said reverse osmosis, which uses pressure to push water through a semipermeable membrane, is more energy-efficient. However, the technology has one drawback: it struggles to treat water saltier than seawater.

Heating water into vapor and then condensing it back into freshwater is another viable solution, but this method requires more energy.

Turning wastewater into coolant

According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day. The waste water generated by certain oil fields in Texas is over thousand fold higher than this amount.

Data centers can become more efficient in their water usage if they reduce stress on local water resources without drastically increasing costs or overall energy demand, according to a recently published study in Water Research.

“We’re not waiting for a futuristic technology to come along and solve this problem for us,” said Vaibhav Bahadur, who is a professor at the University’s Cockrell School of Engineering’s Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering and is one of the leaders of the research.

Bahudur noted that though the desalinations methods are available but they incur a cost. These costs, however, will be a small fraction of a data center’s total energy footprint when compared even with the most energy-intensive water treatment.

Texas oilfields offer alternatives

He proposed turning attention to the Permian Basin. This geological region in West Texas generates approximately 8 billion gallons of produced water per day during oil and gas extraction.

The researcher said this water could be put to better use instead of being transported elsewhere for disposal, where it could pose long-term risks.

“The Permian (Basin) puts out 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools per day, and right now this water is transported over long distances and injected underground. This is problematic in many ways including the risk of seismic activity,” Bahadur said. “We’re also running out of space to bury that water, by as early as 2030. We need to find a way to use it, and cleaning it up for data centers is a great way to do that.”

The research finding becomes significant given that only less than 4 percent of Earth’s water is freshwater, and only a fraction of it, just 0.5 percent, is accessible and safe for human consumption. Additionally, by 2028, water consumption by data centers is expected to reach approximately 33 billion gallons, filling nearly 50,000 Olympic-sized pools, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

For 15 years, America used about the same amount of electricity every year.

This year it will use more than it ever has.

That is the Energy Information Administration's forecast from earlier this month: 4,135 billion kilowatthours in 2026, a record, rising to 4,211 billion in 2027. The agency names two drivers. Data centers, and manufacturing.

The turn came quickly. After a decade and a half of nearly flat consumption, demand has grown 2.1% a year over the last five. In January, EIA noted it was the first time since 2007 that power demand had risen four years in a row.

Texas felt it first. On July 22, ERCOT set a new all-time peak of about 91 gigawatts, clearing the old record from August 2023 by more than 5 gigawatts.

In 2021 I gave a talk called A Ruins to Renaissance Playbook, about reframing America's infrastructure. One of the last slides carried three words. Resilient Electrical Grids.

At the time, demand had been flat for over a decade and the grid was treated as a finished system.

Roads, ports, water and rail each had a moment when the country chose to build ahead of demand. Electricity has reached that moment again.

$IREN 
I’ve been thinking about Sweetwater and I believe the first phase (or at least a big chunk of it) will be developed and financed more closely with $NVDA than the market is currently pricing in.

The “up to 5GW” partnership isn’t a firm offtake, that’s clear. But Sweetwater is explicitly positioned as the flagship site for NVIDIA’s DSX architecture. NVIDIA already has a cloud contract with IREN, a warrant for up to $2.1B at $70, and a clear interest in having large-scale liquid-cooled capacity in ERCOT as a reference.

For $IREN, the CapEx for SW1 comes at a tough time: they’re dealing with the Horizons at Childress, liquid-cooling retrofits in Canada, and the 2027 ramp all at once. A large block of Sweetwater with NVIDIA as an anchor (whether through preferential offtake, stronger prepayments, or some form of JV/joint financing) would make sense for both sides. NVIDIA gets priority capacity and a real DSX showcase, while IREN unlocks part of the data center CapEx and reduces dilution or delay risk.

At the same time, I see IREN focused on actually building IREN Cloud, especially for smaller developers (AI-native startups and enterprise customers that aren’t hyperscalers). The Mirantis acquisition and management’s comments about diversifying the customer base point in that direction. The big offtakes (Microsoft, and potentially NVIDIA at Sweetwater) give them the scale and funding to build the infrastructure, but the longer-term goal seems to be having their own platform that captures more value with a broader mix of customers.

I’m not saying NVIDIA takes 100% of the campus, but the first meaningful phase of Sweetwater makes more sense as a joint project than as just another standard contract.
